questions.prompt: How clearly can your organization trace technology investment and run spend to named strategy objectives?
questions.intent: Assess whether technology spend is linked to the enterprise's named strategy objectives, so that the organization can show leadership what it is buying toward and stop spend that supports nothing.
questions.answerDesign: Select the description that is true for most material technology spend today, not for the best single programme. If the enterprise strategy has no named objectives, choose the fourth option.
questions.adaptiveTrigger: Strategy=Not traced activates value alignment deep dive
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate with the strategy document or objectives list, the investment portfolio or approved-initiative register showing the objective for each item, and the last portfolio review minutes.
questions.findingImplication: L7 Value Leakage / Strategy alignment of technology spend

options.label: Most material technology spend, run and change, is mapped to named strategy objectives; the mapping is reviewed on a regular cycle and used to re-prioritise or stop investments.
Each new material investment must name the strategy objective it supports at approval, but existing run spend is not mapped or reviewed against objectives.
Investments are grouped under broad strategic themes (for example growth, resilience, efficiency) without named objectives or owners.
Strategic fit is described in business cases in general terms, or the enterprise strategy has no named objectives to trace to; the link is not recorded or checked.
We cannot say which strategy objectives most technology spend supports.

scoring.basis: Ordered scale of how fully technology spend is traced to named strategy objectives, from the whole portfolio mapped and reviewed down to not known, with UNKNOWN at the lowest level. Scored on VALUE-01 only. The engine ignores valueDimensionIds, so nothing else is credited. This is the first scored question for VALUE-01, which had none (COVERAGE-MATRIX section 3). The construct follows the FinOps Executive Strategy Alignment capability and the GAO investment framework; the option wording and the steps are LTM's. The 100/80/60/40/20 steps are an LTM convention, not a benchmark; the FinOps Framework gives three stages (Crawl, Walk, Run), not scores. Strategy objectives vary in quality: a mapped portfolio against vague objectives scores high, so this reads traceability, not the quality of the strategy. Complements CORE-19 (evidence required before funding approval) and CORE-44 (whether outcomes are measured afterwards): this asks whether the objective link exists for the whole spend, run included.

questions.answerGuidance: Think of the last time leadership asked what technology spend is for. Use the strategy objectives as the enterprise states them. Answer on current practice, not intended practice.

questionBasis.basis: Scores how fully technology spend is traced to named strategy objectives. FinOps Executive Strategy Alignment connects technology spend, usage and adoption to business strategy and priorities and describes Crawl (limited, ad hoc link to initiatives) through Run (Scopes as the standard lens connecting strategy, funding and accountability). GAO-04-394G expects an investment board to evaluate alignment of IT projects and systems with strategic goals and objectives and to take corrective action (Stage 2) and a portfolio view against strategic goals (Stage 3).

sources.title: FinOps Framework: Executive Strategy Alignment
sources.whatItSays: Capability in the Manage the FinOps Practice domain that connects technology spend, usage and adoption to the organization's business strategy and priorities. Executive Priority Alignment: map technology spend across cloud, SaaS, AI, licensing and data center to the initiatives leaders fund. Enable Strategic Decision Support: a portfolio view so leaders can see how spend maps to strategic priorities. Crawl: insights relate to strategic initiatives in a limited, ad hoc way. Walk: Scopes span several technology categories and are explicitly tied to executive priorities, with a regular governance cadence. Run: Scopes are the standard lens connecting strategy, funding and accountability; FinOps is a required input for major investments; alignment holds through restructuring, M&A and leadership change. The page defines no explicit success measure for tracing spend to objectives. Read through a summarising fetch tool.

sources.title: Information Technology Investment Management: A Framework for Assessing and Improving Process Maturity (GAO-04-394G, version 1.1)
sources.whatItSays: Read from the PDF text (https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-04-394g.pdf), not the product page, which does not mention stages or strategic alignment. Stage 2 (Building the Investment Foundation, Meeting Business Need, PDF p. 45): the investment board periodically evaluates the alignment of its IT projects and systems with the organization's strategic goals and objectives and takes corrective action when misalignment occurs. Stage 3 (Developing a Complete Investment Portfolio, PDF p. 67): taking a portfolio perspective means investments address the strategic goals, objectives and mission and the impact projects have on one another. US federal context, 2004; it describes process maturity, not a measure of traceability.

questionBasis.heuristicReasoning: The five options and the 100/80/60/40/20 steps are LTM's. Neither source gives a ladder or a measure of traceability. The FinOps page itself defines no success measure for tracing spend to objectives, and GAO describes process maturity for a US federal agency in 2004.
questionBasis.notes: First scored VALUE-01 question. Complements CORE-19, CORE-44 and CORE-07 (context, VALUE-01 tag).

questions.needsOwnerReason: Placement. Section 'Value Management' belongs to the opt-in Technology Value area (default areas are now Infrastructure and Applications), so a default run never shows it and VALUE-01 still has no score for most clients. Options: (a) keep it in Value Management (recommended default, no page change); (b) move it to the baseline section 'Cost Governance & Investment' so every client answers it (one more baseline question, 29 not 28, against the 15 to 20 minute executive target; COVERAGE-MATRIX M4 asks for 10 of 16 dimensions scored in executive mode). Also confirm the single question is enough: COVERAGE-MATRIX section 11 says two would be better if the owner wants a firm VALUE-01 score.

questions.prompt: How well does your organization know the fully loaded cost of its internal technology staff and contractors, and how far is it used in decisions?
questions.intent: Assess whether the largest technology cost pool, people, is costed completely enough to compare internal, contractor and managed-service options.
questions.answerDesign: Select the description that matches how technology people cost is known and used today. Fully loaded means more than salary or day rate: include benefits, overheads, tools, facilities and management time.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate with a loaded-rate table by role, the technology payroll and contractor cost extract, and a recent sourcing or business-case decision that used them.
questions.findingImplication: L5 Workforce Leakage / Workforce cost visibility

options.label: Fully loaded cost (pay, benefits, overheads, tools, facilities, management time) is known for both internal staff and contractors by role or team and is used in sourcing, staffing and business-case decisions.
Fully loaded cost is known for both internal staff and contractors and reported, but is not routinely used in sourcing or investment decisions.
Fully loaded cost is known for one group only, usually contractors from invoices, while internal staff are costed at an average salary or headcount budget.
Only headcount budgets and contractor invoice totals are known; no loaded cost per role or team is calculated.
We cannot say what technology staff and contractors cost in total.

scoring.basis: Ordered scale of how completely technology people cost is known and used, down to not known, with UNKNOWN at the lowest level. LTM heuristic: the options and the 100/80/60/40/20 steps are LTM's. The 100/80/60/40/20 steps are an LTM convention, not a benchmark; the FinOps Framework gives three stages (Crawl, Walk, Run), not scores. No published scale for workforce cost visibility was found. The TBM Staffing cost pool (internal labour plus staff augmentation) and the FinOps Unit Economics reference to fully loaded costs support the construct only; the FinOps wording is about unit cost of technology resources, not workforce. Gated on WORKFORCE or EXTERNAL in CORE-01 because there is no not-applicable option. Complements ADP-18 (how the internal and contractor mix is decided) and CORE-35 (capacity alignment): this asks whether the cost basis for those decisions exists. Do not present as independent evidence with ADP-18.

questions.answerGuidance: Include permanent staff and contractors engaged to do technology work. Consider whether the figure would survive a finance review.

questionBasis.basis: Scores whether fully loaded internal and contractor cost is known and used. The TBM Staffing cost pool separates internal labour (salaries, benefits and related costs) from staff augmentation and time-and-material contractors, and FinOps Unit Economics describes unit views that include fully loaded costs at Walk and Run.

sources.title: TBM Taxonomy 5.0.1: Staffing cost pool
sources.whatItSays: Staffing includes salaries, benefits and other costs of internal personnel, plus Time & Material contractor and staff augmentation resources; it excludes consultant and managed service resources. Sub-pools: Internal Labor, Staff Augmentation (T&M contractors), Other Operating. No separate Contractors sub-pool. Read through a summarising fetch tool, first 100,000 of 204,029 characters; the page states no licence or reuse terms in the text read.

sources.title: FinOps Framework: Unit Economics
sources.whatItSays: Unit Economics connects what an organization spends on technology to the value it creates. Metrics can be resource-efficiency measures (cost per GB, per vCPU, per token) or business-unit measures (per transaction, per customer, per case resolved; revenue and per-tenant views). Crawl: usually one technology category, technical metrics tied to direct variable cost, business outcome data not yet correlated. Walk: includes public cloud, SaaS use, data centers and others; unit views begin to include fully loaded costs; cost to serve becomes more trustworthy; decision use is moderate. Run: every operational Scope has defined unit metrics across all technology categories, including fully loaded costs, and unit economics shape build-versus-buy, architecture, workload placement, migration, sourcing and pricing decisions early. Read through a summarising fetch tool.

questionBasis.heuristicReasoning: The ladder and the steps are LTM's judgement: a CIO who cannot cost people on a like-for-like basis cannot judge build, buy or borrow, and the largest cost pool of many estates should not rest on salary alone. The cited sources support the cost-category split and the idea of fully loaded cost; neither describes a workforce cost-visibility maturity scale. This is not a benchmark.
questionBasis.notes: Second scored COST-06 question with ADP-63 (COST-06 would have four: CORE-35, ADP-18, ADP-62, ADP-63).

questions.needsOwnerReason: None beyond the gate: it is shown only when the footprint (CORE-01) names WORKFORCE or EXTERNAL, unlike CORE-35 and ADP-18, which are ungated.

questions.prompt: How is demand for technology contractors governed: who approves it, what rates apply and how are long-running roles reviewed?
questions.intent: Assess whether contractor use is controlled at the point of demand, at the rate paid and over time, rather than only audited after the spend.
questions.answerDesign: Select the description that best matches how contractors are requested, priced and reviewed today. If you use no contractors, leave this question unanswered.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate with the contractor request and approval process, the rate card or framework agreement, the contractor register with start dates, and any conversion review record.
questions.findingImplication: L5 Workforce Leakage / Contractor demand governance

options.label: Each contractor request needs a documented need and approval, rates follow a rate card or framework agreement, and long-running roles are reviewed at set intervals for conversion to employees, fixed-price work or a managed service.
Requests are approved and rates are controlled by a rate card or framework, but long-running roles are not systematically reviewed for conversion.
Requests are approved by the hiring manager or budget holder, rates are negotiated case by case, and there is no conversion review.
Teams engage contractors with little central approval or rate control.
We cannot say how many contractors are engaged, at what rates or for how long.

scoring.basis: Ordered scale across the three controls named in the prompt (approval, rates, conversion), from all three in place to none and not known, with UNKNOWN at the lowest level. LTM heuristic: the ladder and the 100/80/60/40/20 steps are LTM's; no published scale for contractor governance was found. The 100/80/60/40/20 steps are an LTM convention, not a benchmark; the FinOps Framework gives three stages (Crawl, Walk, Run), not scores. Dependency: there is no 'we use no contractors' option, and a not-applicable answer cannot be scored. Gating on WORKFORCE or EXTERNAL narrows the audience but a client with no contractors would still be scored low if it answers; the answerDesign tells such clients to leave it unanswered, and an unanswered question is not scored. Owner may prefer a CORE-36 based gate (the share of workforce supplied externally is already asked) but applicableWhen supports only CORE-01 options. Complements ADP-18 (how the internal and contractor balance is decided: strategy level) and CORE-36 (external share, context): this asks about day-to-day demand control. Wording overlap with ADP-18's 'reviewed' is small but real: ADP-18 asks whether the mix is reviewed against economics, this asks about approval, rates and conversion of individual roles.

questions.answerGuidance: Consider time-and-material and staff-augmentation contractors, not consultants or managed services priced as an outcome. Answer on current practice for most contractor spend.

questionBasis.basis: Scores approval, rate control and conversion review for contractor demand. The TBM Staffing cost pool names staff augmentation and time-and-material contractors as a distinct cost from internal labour and from managed services, which is the boundary this question uses. No published source for the approval, rate-card and conversion ladder was found.

sources.title: TBM Taxonomy 5.0.1: Staffing cost pool
sources.whatItSays: Staffing includes salaries, benefits and other costs of internal personnel, plus Time & Material contractor and staff augmentation resources; it excludes consultant and managed service resources. Sub-pools: Internal Labor, Staff Augmentation (T&M contractors), Other Operating. No separate Contractors sub-pool. Read through a summarising fetch tool, first 100,000 of 204,029 characters; the page states no licence or reuse terms in the text read.

questionBasis.heuristicReasoning: Approval at the point of demand, a controlled rate and a periodic look at long-running roles are the three levers a CIO or procurement lead usually names for contractor spend; ordering them by how many are in place is LTM judgement. The TBM source supports only the cost category, not the controls or their order. No benchmark of contractor premium over employee cost is used or implied. Conversion is not always better: a short, specialist need is correctly met by a contractor.
questionBasis.notes: Both Q2 questions feed COST-06 only. Not independent of ADP-18 on the same theme.

questions.needsOwnerReason: Clients with no contractors have no not-applicable option (the same gap as ADP-18). Options: (a) accept, with the 'leave unanswered' instruction (recommended); (b) add a gate on a CORE-36 answer, which needs an engine change because applicableWhen supports CORE-01 options only.

questions.prompt: How well does your organization know what end-user devices and workplace software cost per user?
questions.intent: Assess whether end-user and workplace technology, the main infrastructure cost of many software-heavy and outsourced estates, is understood per user and by type of user.
questions.answerDesign: Select the description that matches how end-user cost is known today. Include laptops, desktops, mobile devices, workplace software licences and end-user support; exclude data-centre and cloud infrastructure.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate with the device and workplace-software spend by user type, user counts from HR or the directory, and the support cost per user.
questions.findingImplication: L2 Consumption Leakage / End-user cost per user

options.label: Fully loaded cost per user (devices, workplace software, support) is known by type of user (for example office, frontline, specialist) and is used to set standards or challenge them.
A single average cost per user is known and reviewed at least annually, but not by type of user.
Device, workplace-software and support costs are known separately, but not combined into a cost per user.
Only a total end-user or workplace technology budget is known.
We cannot say what end-user technology costs per user.

scoring.basis: Ordered scale of how completely end-user cost is known per user, from by-persona and used down to not known, with UNKNOWN at the lowest level. Scored on COST-05, as the owner-approved Q3 brief proposed ('COST-05 or a new workplace item'); the closest TBM element, the End User tower, is not one of the towers the taxonomy mapping names for COST-05 (Data Center, Compute, Storage, Network), so the mapping is a judgement. LTM heuristic: the ladder and steps are LTM's. The 100/80/60/40/20 steps are an LTM convention, not a benchmark; the FinOps Framework gives three stages (Crawl, Walk, Run), not scores. Gated on END_USER in CORE-01 because there is no not-applicable option. Overlaps in theme with ADP-06 and CORE-26 (SaaS overlap and licence counts) only where workplace software is a SaaS product: those ask about overlap and reclamation, this asks about cost per user. Complements ADP-65 (lifecycle and refresh).

questions.answerGuidance: A user is anyone issued a device or workplace-software licence by the organization. Answer on current practice, not on what could be built.

questionBasis.basis: Scores whether end-user and workplace cost is known per user. The TBM Taxonomy names an End User tower (workspace devices, mobile devices, help desk, deskside support) and FinOps Unit Economics describes unit metrics across technology categories including SaaS use, at Walk and Run.

sources.title: TBM Taxonomy 5.0.1: End User tower
sources.whatItSays: End User tower: resources enabling individual productivity, including user computing equipment, mobile technology, workspace devices and centralized support channels. Sub-towers: Conferencing & AV, Deskside Support, Help Desk, Mobile Devices, Network Printers, Workspace, and End User Software (marked retired). Workspace covers desktops, laptops, thin clients and peripherals and excludes software, labor and support. The visible page names no cost-per-user or per-device metric. Read through a summarising fetch tool, first 100,000 of 204,029 characters.

Metrics can be resource-efficiency measures (cost per GB, per vCPU, per token) or business-unit measures (per transaction, per customer, per case resolved; revenue and per-tenant views). Crawl: usually one technology category, technical metrics tied to direct variable cost, business outcome data not yet correlated. Walk: includes public cloud, SaaS use, data centers and others; unit views begin to include fully loaded costs; cost to serve becomes more trustworthy; decision use is moderate. Run: every operational Scope has defined unit metrics across all technology categories, including fully loaded costs, and unit economics shape build-versus-buy, architecture, workload placement, migration, sourcing and pricing decisions early. Read through a summarising fetch tool.

questionBasis.heuristicReasoning: The cost-per-user ladder is LTM's judgement: cost per user is the standard unit of measure for workplace technology in practice, but no source read gives a scale or a benchmark value, and the TBM page as read names no cost-per-user metric. The sources support the tower and the unit-metric idea only. No cost-per-user benchmark is used or implied; published figures vary by industry and user type and none was verified.
questionBasis.notes: First of two questions on the End User tower, which CORE-01 offers (END_USER) and CORE-05 lists but no question asked about.

questions.needsOwnerReason: Dimension and section. Scored on COST-05 (recommended: no page change, lifts COST-05 for SaaS-heavy and outsourced clients), versus a new workplace dimension (breaks the 16-dimension count and the report). Section is the existing 'Infrastructure & Operations'; a gated question is shown whenever the footprint names the estate (selectQuestions in cost-iq-v10.html), so no focus-area change is needed. Confirm.

questions.prompt: How are the lifecycle and refresh of end-user devices and workplace software decided and controlled?
questions.intent: Assess whether end-user refresh is a managed cost and risk decision or happens by default, since refresh cycle length is the main driver of device cost over time.
questions.answerDesign: Select the description that best matches how devices and workplace software are refreshed today. Answer for the majority of devices.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate with the device inventory (count, age, model), the refresh policy, and the last three years of device purchases against the policy.

options.label: A device and workplace-software lifecycle policy (refresh cycle, standard models, extension or reuse, disposal or resale) is set on cost and risk, tracked in an asset inventory, and exceptions need approval.
A refresh cycle is defined and mostly applied, but exceptions are common or cost and risk are not reviewed against it.
Devices are tracked in an inventory, but replacement is driven mainly by warranty, vendor support end or operating-system end of life.
Devices are replaced mainly on failure or on request, with no reliable inventory.
We cannot say how many devices are in service or how old they are.

scoring.basis: Ordered scale of how deliberately end-user lifecycle is governed, from policy set on cost and risk with an inventory down to replacement on failure and not known, with UNKNOWN at the lowest level. LTM heuristic: the ladder and steps are LTM's; I found no published scale. The 100/80/60/40/20 steps are an LTM convention, not a benchmark; the FinOps Framework gives three stages (Crawl, Walk, Run), not scores. Longer is not always better: a short cycle can be right for security or productivity reasons, so the scale reads whether the cycle is decided and tracked, not its length. Gated on END_USER in CORE-01. Wording overlap: CORE-33 asks what drives infrastructure capacity planning and refresh (ungated, data-centre framing) and ADP-12 asks the on-premises share nearing end of life (context); this asks about devices and workplace software only, so it complements both. Do not present as independent evidence with CORE-33.

questions.answerGuidance: Consider laptops, desktops and mobile devices and the workplace software that runs on them. Answer on current practice.

questionBasis.basis: Scores how deliberately end-user device and workplace-software lifecycle is governed. The TBM Taxonomy End User tower names workspace devices, mobile devices and support as resource components, which gives the scope. No source read describes refresh governance.

sources.title: TBM Taxonomy 5.0.1: End User tower
sources.whatItSays: End User tower: resources enabling individual productivity, including user computing equipment, mobile technology, workspace devices and centralized support channels. Sub-towers: Conferencing & AV, Deskside Support, Help Desk, Mobile Devices, Network Printers, Workspace, and End User Software (marked retired). Workspace covers desktops, laptops, thin clients and peripherals and excludes software, labor and support. The visible page names no cost-per-user or per-device metric. Read through a summarising fetch tool, first 100,000 of 204,029 characters.

questionBasis.heuristicReasoning: A defined refresh policy, an inventory, and a refresh driven by cost and risk rather than failure follow common asset-management practice; ordering them is LTM judgement. ISO/IEC 19770-1 (IT asset management) is relevant in principle but its clauses were not opened (iso.org returned HTTP 403 earlier on 3 Nov 2026), so it is not cited. No device-lifetime or refresh-cost figure is used.

questions.needsOwnerReason: Same dimension and section choice as ADP-64; no separate decision.

questions.prompt: How well does your organization know the unit cost of its own infrastructure, such as a virtual machine, a terabyte or a rack, and how far is it shown to consumers and compared with alternatives?
questions.intent: Assess whether internally run infrastructure is costed per unit, made visible to its consumers and tested against other ways of running the same workload.
questions.answerDesign: Select the description that matches current practice for most internally run infrastructure (data centre, private cloud, virtualised estate, colocation). Showing costs back to consumers counts as much as formally charging them.
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate with the unit-cost calculation by service (VM, storage, rack), the showback or chargeback report, and the last comparison against a cloud or colocation alternative.
questions.findingImplication: L1 Visibility Leakage / Internal infrastructure unit cost

options.label: Unit cost (per VM, per terabyte, per rack or per core) is calculated from full cost (hardware, facilities, power, licences, labour), shown or charged back to consumers, and compared with cloud, colocation or hosted alternatives at least annually.
Unit cost is calculated from full cost and shown or charged back to consumers, but is not compared with alternatives.
Unit cost is calculated for some services for planning, but consumers do not see it and it is not compared with alternatives.
Only the total infrastructure budget or depreciation is known; no unit cost is calculated.
We cannot say what a virtual machine, a terabyte or a rack costs us.

scoring.basis: Ordered scale of how fully internal infrastructure unit cost is known, shown and compared, from compared with alternatives down to not known, with UNKNOWN at the lowest level. Scored on COST-05 only; COST-01 is not credited because the engine would then count one answer in two dimensions (and valueDimensionIds is ignored). The construct follows FinOps Unit Economics (data centres at Walk; unit metrics shape workload placement at Run) and Architecting & Workload Placement (value comparison across placement options including data center and private cloud). The ladder and steps are LTM's. The 100/80/60/40/20 steps are an LTM convention, not a benchmark; the FinOps Framework gives three stages (Crawl, Walk, Run), not scores. FinOps Invoicing & Chargeback says chargeback is optional and neither showback nor chargeback is more mature; the ladder therefore credits showback or chargeback equally. Gated on ON_PREM, PRIVATE_CLOUD, VMWARE or COLO in CORE-01 because there is no not-applicable option. Overlaps: CORE-13 (the level at which cost is understood, whose top option names unit economics) is general; ADP-09 (virtualization licensing, infrastructure and alternatives, gated) asks about platform renewal analysis; ADP-11 and ADP-37 ask about capacity utilisation; ADP-13 asks about colocation contract economics. This question complements all of them by asking for unit cost and comparison; it should not be read as independent evidence with ADP-09.

questions.answerGuidance: Include the full cost of running the unit, not only hardware depreciation or the hosting fee. Answer for most of the internally run estate, not the best-managed platform.

questionBasis.basis: Scores whether internal infrastructure unit cost is known, shown to consumers and compared with alternatives. FinOps Unit Economics extends unit metrics (for example cost per GB, per vCPU) to data centers at Walk and says unit economics shape workload placement at Run; FinOps Architecting & Workload Placement calls for value comparison across placement options such as public cloud, data center and private cloud; FinOps Invoicing & Chargeback says showback is required and chargeback is optional.

sources.title: FinOps Framework: Unit Economics
sources.whatItSays: Unit Economics connects what an organization spends on technology to the value it creates. Metrics can be resource-efficiency measures (cost per GB, per vCPU, per token) or business-unit measures (per transaction, per customer, per case resolved; revenue and per-tenant views). Crawl: usually one technology category, technical metrics tied to direct variable cost, business outcome data not yet correlated. Walk: includes public cloud, SaaS use, data centers and others; unit views begin to include fully loaded costs; cost to serve becomes more trustworthy; decision use is moderate. Run: every operational Scope has defined unit metrics across all technology categories, including fully loaded costs, and unit economics shape build-versus-buy, architecture, workload placement, migration, sourcing and pricing decisions early. Read through a summarising fetch tool.

sources.title: FinOps Framework: Architecting & Workload Placement
sources.whatItSays: Covers designing solutions with cost in mind and choosing where workloads run within and across technology categories, connecting placement options to business unit metrics. Build the Decision Case calls for value comparisons across placement options such as public cloud, data center and private cloud; inputs include infrastructure cost, support and run cost, and migration cost. Crawl: case-by-case with rules of thumb and no documented trade-off model. Walk: a documented model weighs cost, value, sovereignty, resilience and sustainability. Run: built is tracked against modelled and variance feeds back. It recommends tracking unit cost trends against a business unit metric. Colocation is not mentioned and the page does not define on-premises boundaries. Read through a summarising fetch tool.

sources.title: FinOps Framework: Invoicing & Chargeback
sources.whatItSays: Showback (showing groups the costs of their own scope) is required in every FinOps practice; chargeback (formal posting to accounting budgets) is optional, depends on accounting policy, and the page says neither is more mature than the other. Crawl: charged on estimates with material variance, spreadsheets. Run: teams see direct and allocated shared costs from actual consumption and chargeback is automated. The page does not address on-premises or data-centre costs specifically. Read through a summarising fetch tool.

sources.title: TBM Taxonomy 5.0.1: Compute and Data Center towers
sources.whatItSays: Compute has sub-towers such as Servers, Converged Infrastructure, Mainframe, HPC and AI Compute; Data Center has Enterprise Data Center and Other Facilities. The part of the page read names no unit-cost metric (per VM, per terabyte) for these towers; the KPI section was not in the text read, so absence is not established. Cited only for the towers, not for any unit-cost method.

questionBasis.heuristicReasoning: The framework sources support the construct (unit cost for data centres, comparison of placement options, showback). They give no ladder and no unit-cost value. The five options and the steps are LTM's. TBM is cited for the towers only; the part of the page read names no unit-cost metric for them (absence not established), so none is attributed to TBM. Colocation is not mentioned by the FinOps placement page, so including COLO in the gate is LTM judgement.
questionBasis.notes: No finding trigger proposed. Complements CORE-13, ADP-09, ADP-11, ADP-13, ADP-37.

questions.prompt: How far does your organization track technology cost per unit of business output, such as per transaction, per employee or per revenue unit?
questions.intent: Assess whether technology cost is related to what the business produces, so that a rising bill can be told apart from rising volume.
questions.answerDesign: Select the description that matches current practice. A unit of business output is whatever the business counts: transactions, customers, orders, employees or revenue.
questions.adaptiveTrigger: UnitCost=No activates technology productivity deep dive
questions.evidenceImplication: Validate with the unit-cost report, the denominator data source and a recent budget or investment decision that cites it.
questions.findingImplication: L7 Value Leakage / Technology cost per unit of output

options.label: Technology cost per unit of business output (for example per transaction, per customer, per employee or per revenue unit) is tracked for the main business services, trended over time and used in budget and investment decisions.
Technology cost per unit of business output is tracked and reported to leadership for at least one major service, but not used in budget or investment decisions.
One organisation-wide ratio, for example technology spend as a share of revenue or per employee, is calculated, but nothing by service or business output.
Technology cost per unit of business output is not tracked, though it could be worked out on request.
We do not know whether, or how, technology cost is related to business output.

scoring.basis: Ordered scale of how fully technology cost is related to business output, from used in decisions down to not known, with UNKNOWN at the lowest level. Scored on VALUE-04 only. VALUE-04 now holds CORE-34 (manual-effort share) and CORE-35 (workforce alignment), both shared with cost dimensions; this question is the first that feeds VALUE-04 from an output-based measure (COVERAGE-MATRIX section 11, Q5). The construct follows FinOps Unit Economics (business denominators per transaction, customer or case; revenue views) and Executive Strategy Alignment (unit measures such as cost per transaction or per active user); the ladder and steps are LTM's. The 100/80/60/40/20 steps are an LTM convention, not a benchmark; the FinOps Framework gives three stages (Crawl, Walk, Run), not scores. A top-level ratio such as IT spend as a share of revenue is shown as a weaker rung and no benchmark value is used. Overlaps: CORE-13 (the level at which cost is understood, top option mentions unit economics) is about cost allocation; ADP-66 asks the same idea for internal infrastructure only. Complements both; do not present as independent evidence with CORE-13.

questions.answerGuidance: Pick the rung that matches what is routinely reported today, not what could be calculated if asked.

questionBasis.basis: Scores whether technology cost per unit of business output is tracked and used. FinOps Unit Economics connects technology spend to the value it creates, lists business denominators (per transaction, per customer, per case resolved; revenue views), and at Run applies unit metrics across all technology categories and uses them in build-versus-buy, architecture and placement decisions. FinOps Executive Strategy Alignment names cost per transaction, cost to serve and cost per active user as executive-level unit measures.

sources.title: FinOps Framework: Unit Economics
sources.whatItSays: Unit Economics connects what an organization spends on technology to the value it creates. Metrics can be resource-efficiency measures (cost per GB, per vCPU, per token) or business-unit measures (per transaction, per customer, per case resolved; revenue and per-tenant views). Crawl: usually one technology category, technical metrics tied to direct variable cost, business outcome data not yet correlated. Walk: includes public cloud, SaaS use, data centers and others; unit views begin to include fully loaded costs; cost to serve becomes more trustworthy; decision use is moderate. Run: every operational Scope has defined unit metrics across all technology categories, including fully loaded costs, and unit economics shape build-versus-buy, architecture, workload placement, migration, sourcing and pricing decisions early. Read through a summarising fetch tool.

sources.title: FinOps Framework: Executive Strategy Alignment
sources.whatItSays: Capability in the Manage the FinOps Practice domain that connects technology spend, usage and adoption to the organization's business strategy and priorities. Executive Priority Alignment: map technology spend across cloud, SaaS, AI, licensing and data center to the initiatives leaders fund. Enable Strategic Decision Support: a portfolio view so leaders can see how spend maps to strategic priorities. Crawl: insights relate to strategic initiatives in a limited, ad hoc way. Walk: Scopes span several technology categories and are explicitly tied to executive priorities, with a regular governance cadence. Run: Scopes are the standard lens connecting strategy, funding and accountability; FinOps is a required input for major investments; alignment holds through restructuring, M&A and leadership change. The page defines no explicit success measure for tracing spend to objectives. Read through a summarising fetch tool.

questionBasis.heuristicReasoning: Both pages give the idea and the denominators; neither gives a ladder or a target. The five options and the steps are LTM's. The page says the most actionable view is usually a trend within a defined scope, which the top two options reflect, but a trend of a bad unit can still be a bad answer, so the scale reads practice, not performance. No unit-cost benchmark is used.
questionBasis.notes: Third scored VALUE-04 question; the first not shared with a cost dimension.
